### Introduction

This research is part of a series of reports which aim to collate and review current 
evidence on the potential environmental impacts and social implications of five 
greenhouse gas (GHG) removal technologies: ocean alkalinity enhancement, enhanced 
rock weathering (ERW), biochar, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), 
and direct air carbon capture and storage (DACCS). This briefing is one of a series of 
reviews that presents a snapshot of the published evidence for the environmental 
impacts of greenhouse gas removal (GGR) methods up to Autumn 2022. It considers 
bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS). 
This review will summarise current understanding of the wider environmental impacts 
for the deployment at scale of GGR methods, individually and in combination with 
others, up to 2050. It will discuss the consequences for environmental regulation with a 
focus on the Environment Agency’s current regulatory role including the Environmental 
Permitting Regulations 2016 and the Water Resources Act 1991. It will identify 
uncertainties in the evidence and the need for further research to consider individual 
methods and their interactions with others as part of a portfolio. 
Literature searches were conducted in October 2022 for relevant papers using Scopus, 
with abstracts screened for relevance on environmental impacts from one or more parts 
of the BECCS process from biomass production to carbon capture and storage (CCS). 
Citations within selected papers were also identified, followed up, and reviewed for 
relevance as well as grey literature published by BEIS, Defra, the Forestry Commission, 
and other Government departments and agencies. 
A non-technical summary of this research is also provided as a separate document. 

### Overview of greenhouse gas removal methods

Updates to the Climate Change Act 2008 committed the UK to a 100% reduction in emissions by the year 2050 relative to 1990 levels (RS and RAE 2018). It is recognised that emissions will never be reduced to zero and therefore atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) will need to be removed from the atmosphere to offset the remaining emissions (BEIS 2021a). Modelled estimates of residual emissions vary from 100 to 160 Mt CO2 pa (CCC 2020, RS and RAE 2018). While mitigation methods such as low carbon energy production aim to reduce the levels of CO2 emitted to the atmosphere, Greenhouse Gas Removal (GGR) methods, also

called negative emissions technologies (NET), do the reverse by taking it from the atmosphere into long-term storage within terrestrial and marine systems (NASEM 2019). To achieve the reduction in emissions required by 2050, GGR methods including traditional land-based practices such as afforestation and engineered infrastructure such as bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) will need to be deployed at an unprecedented speed and scale. GGR methods cannot be deployed at scale without wider consequences for the environment and public health (RS and RAE 2018, NASEEM 2019). Potential environmental impacts1 include direct pollution emissions to air, soil, and water; consumption of limited environmental resources such as water and land; and production of liquid and solid wastes. It is important that these potential hazards are clearly understood at the outset of planning and commissioning a strategic approach for the UK to maximise CO2 removal and minimise wider environmental risk. Monitoring and control measures implemented by environmental regulation will also be needed to manage the wider environmental impacts of GGR methods during their operational lifetime.

### Overview of BECCS

#### Description

BECCS utilises biomass for energy, capturing the CO2 emissions from combustion and storing them to provide life cycle GGR (RS and RAE 2018). Energy can be supplied as electricity, heat, or as gas or liquid fuels (Shahbaz et al. 2021). One of the policy advantages of BECCS is seen to be a cost-effective producer of low-carbon energy, which helps to offset the cost of CO2 removals (Fajardy and MacDowell 2018 and 2020, Zhang et al. 2020). Asibor et al. (2021) noted that BECCS was deployable under a wide range of climatic conditions and geographical areas, although cost optimal sites (proximity to biomass sources and geological storage locations) would be preferred. This economic advantage and seemingly robust flexibility means that it is often predicted to be the largest contributor to CO2 removals in various integrated assessment models out

to 2050 (RS and RAE 2018, CCC 2020, and BEIS 2021a) and one of the strategic drivers for scaling its implementation is the optimisation of the biomass supply chain to minimise energy generation cost. The economic case for BECCS may conflict with its GGR potential. For example, one option to reduce energy cost is to improve power efficiency per tonne of biomass consumed, which conversely reduces the amount of CO2 captured overall (you burn less biomass to meet your energy requirements). In a recent review by BEIS (2021a), the technological readiness level (TRL) of BECCS was considered to range from 5 to 7 (TRL 9 being the most developed) with production of heat and energy considered the most advanced.2 However, Brack and King (2021) observed that despite its demonstration at full-scale, only one commercial BECCS plant was operable by 2019 (located in the USA). The authors noted that a few bioethanol plants had also been established to capture CO2, but for use in enhanced oil recovery rather than for long-term storage.

BECCS is presented as a simple concept (Figure 1a), which belies its complexity (Figure 
1b). There are several integrated components to BECCS: (i) biomass production 
including harvest and transportation, (ii) pelletisation and transportation, (iii) biomass 
transformation to generate energy and fuels, and (iv) carbon capture and storage. As 
shown in Figure 2 (after Jeswani et al. 2022), each component has several possible 
configurations that significantly affect its overall potential environmental impact (for 
example, the use of energy crops compared with agricultural and forestry residues for 
biomass production). Installations can run on biomass alone and in combination with 
fossil fuels. 
Combustion is one of the major processes used to convert biomass energy into 
electricity and heat (Shahbaz et al. 2021). In combustion, biomass is burned in air, 
releasing heat and CO2. It is considered one of the most developed forms of energy 
production from biomass and is central to climate change mitigation and, when 
combined with CCS, removal of CO2 from the atmosphere. In the UK, the fitting of CCS 
to existing biomass units at the Drax Power Station in North Yorkshire has been 
commissioned. 
Gasification involves the thermal decomposition of biomass at elevated temperatures 
with a controlled amount of oxidising agent such as steam and air/oxygen to produce a 
mixture of gases known as syngas (Shahbaz et al. 2021). Syngas consists of hydrogen, 
carbon monoxide, CO2, methane, and nitrogen. Steam is often used as a gasifier 
because the syngas has a higher hydrogen content. Syngas is the feedstock for a range 
of fuel and energy production options including direct burn, production of ammonia and 
urea, synthetic natural gas, petrol, diesel, and jet fuel, and bioethanol and biomethanol. 
Gasification technologies are considered ready for commercialisation. 
Pyrolysis is the heating of biomass in the absence of oxygen to produce a solid biochar 
and liquid/gaseous fuels (Shahbaz et al. 2021). Pyrolysis plants are at the full-scale 
commercial stage, although the use of biochar to sequester carbon in soil is still being 
demonstrated. Biochar is another potential GGR method that uses biomass, and is 
described in a separate summary in this series.
